Cannect:
Simplifying Biotech Traceability

Designing an intelligent traceability tool for a compliance-driven biotechnology B2B platform, reducing critical task completion time by 83%.

Scope

Context

A platform where errors aren't an option

Cannect is an intelligent traceability tool built for a biotechnology company operating in a heavily regulated B2B environment. The platform handles the tracking of biological samples, processes, and compliance documentation — the kind of domain where precision, auditability, and workflow clarity are non-negotiable.

The users are technical professionals: laboratory staff, quality assurance teams, and operations managers — working under strict regulatory requirements. Every interaction with the platform carries real consequences: an unclear interface isn't just frustrating, it creates compliance risk.

Problem

Too much information, too little clarity

The existing interface had accumulated significant complexity over time. Dense information layouts, inconsistent patterns, and workflows that didn't match how users actually performed their tasks. The most critical flows were taking users approximately 30 seconds to complete steps that should have been near-instant.

In a compliance-driven environment, this wasn't just a UX problem. Cognitive overload increases error rates. Slow task completion affects operational throughput. And unclear validation feedback makes it harder for users to trust the system.

The core challenge

How do you simplify a genuinely complex domain without removing the precision and control that technical users depend on? The goal was clarity without oversimplification: making the interface faster without hiding information that matters.

My role

End-to-end design ownership

As UX/UI Lead, I owned the design process from research to final hand-off:

  • Coordinating and facilitating UX research and benchmarking at multiple project stages
  • Defining the information architecture for the redesigned traceability flows
  • Designing and iterating wireframes through to high-fidelity prototypes
  • Validating solutions with users before finalising design decisions
  • Aligning design decisions with the platform's technical constraints
  • Collaborating with engineering on hand-off and implementation

Process

Research first, then design

Before touching the interface, we needed to understand the real workflows, not what the product specification said, but what users actually did. The biotechnology domain is specialised enough that assumptions would have been dangerous.

We ran research sessions at multiple project stages: initial discovery to map task flows and pain points, mid-process to validate early directions, and pre-launch to confirm the final design solved the actual problems.

Benchmarking informed the structural decisions: how comparable platforms in regulated industries handle dense information, how validation patterns work in technical B2B tools, and where we needed to deviate from convention.

User flow mapping, traceability task analysis

Key design decisions

What we changed and why

Decision 01

Progressive disclosure over full density

The original interface displayed all available information simultaneously. We restructured around progressive disclosure — surfacing only what users needed at each step, with detail available on demand. This reduced visual noise without removing access to the data.

Decision 02

Task-oriented navigation over data-oriented navigation

Users were navigating between sections to perform what was conceptually a single task. We restructured the flow to match the user's mental model — the task, not the database structure. This is one of the primary reasons task completion time dropped so significantly.

Decision 03

Explicit, context-aware validation states

In a compliance environment, users need to know not just that something is wrong, but specifically what to do about it. We designed explicit validation feedback that guided users to resolution rather than just flagging errors.

Before / after: key workflow redesign

Final solution

Precision without friction

The redesigned Cannect interface maintains the full complexity of the domain. All the data, all the validation, all the traceability requirements — while making that complexity navigable. Tasks that previously required users to hold multiple pieces of information in their heads simultaneously now follow a clear, step-by-step structure.

The design system established during this project provided a consistent foundation for future development — scalable components that engineering could implement faithfully and that the design team could extend without divergence.

Final Cannect interface — traceability dashboard

Outcome

83% faster. Same precision.

The primary success metric was task completion time on the critical traceability workflow. It went from approximately 30 seconds to 5 seconds — an 83% reduction. This is a meaningful number in an operational context where the same action is repeated many times daily.

Beyond the quantitative result, user satisfaction increased measurably. Users reported feeling more confident in the interface — not just faster, but more in control. In a compliance environment, that sense of clarity and control is a product quality in itself.

Reflection

What I would do next

This project reinforced something I believe strongly: in complex, technical B2B domains, the most important design work is structural — information architecture and workflow design — not visual. Getting the structure right was what drove the 83% improvement. The visual layer followed from that.

Given more time, I would have pushed further on a more robust usability testing programme at the prototype stage, and a deeper exploration of how to surface compliance status at a glance — so users could quickly assess the state of a batch before diving into individual tasks.

Lots management table: each lot shows its current stage (Propagación, Secado, Floración, Curado) with color-coded status badges, reducing the time to identify critical lots.

Lot detail view: complete traceability timeline showing the 5-stage lifecycle (Lote de semilla, Propagación, Vegetación, Floración, Cosecha) with subdivision tracking and export to laboratory.
